picks.headline: U.S. Department of Justice Files Legal Brief Urging Court to Find AI Training to Be Fair Use
picks.excerpt: In a 20-page 'Statement of Interest,' lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice told the judge presiding over a closely watched lawsuit that requiring “paid licensing” would “put U.S. AI companies at a competitive disadvantage.” A direct hit on how authors and publishers can price their work as training data.
picks.rationale: The federal government taking a side on whether AI training is fair use resets the licensing leverage every author and publisher has been negotiating with.

picks.headline: Anthropic Copyright Settlement: Publishers Are Making Incorrect Claims on Authors’ Payouts
picks.excerpt: Authors in the Anthropic class action began receiving settlement notices this week — and some publishers are telling their authors they are entitled to a share when the settlement terms say otherwise. A practical guide to who actually owns the AI-training payout.
picks.rationale: Money is moving this week and authors are being told the wrong thing about their own claim — the most immediately actionable item in the pool.

picks.headline: Google rolls out AI chatbots for books, with permission from publishers and authors
picks.excerpt: Readers of participating Google Play Books titles can now query the text and generate infographics, audio overviews, quizzes and other interactive features — with publisher and author opt-in.
picks.rationale: The first at-scale consumer AI layer sitting inside purchased trade books, and it runs on an opt-in rights decision publishers have to make now.

picks.headline: The AI ‘Ghosts’ Contaminating Academic Publishing
picks.excerpt: “The academic record is being quietly haunted” by nonexistent researchers with names like Elena Vasquez and Marcus Chen — hallucinated co-authors now propagating through published papers and citations.
picks.rationale: Original reporting on a concrete failure mode — fabricated authors entering the permanent citation record — that editors can screen for tomorrow.

picks.headline: Top WSJ Editor Approves AI-Assisted Writing, Says AI Is a “Fact of Modern Life”
picks.excerpt: The Wall Street Journal is giving opinion authors the go-ahead to use AI in the writing process without requiring AI disclosures — a marker for how writing craft norms are shifting.
picks.rationale: A major outlet dropping the disclosure requirement moves the default norm writers and editors are held to, not just the tooling.
